questions.question: What are the REST architectural constraints? What makes an API truly RESTful?
questions.title: REST Architectural Constraints — What Makes an API Truly RESTful
questions.direct_answer: **REST** has 6 architectural constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, and optional code-on-demand. Most 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs — true REST requires **HATEOAS** which few implement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know REST is an architectural style, not just HTTP+JSON
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Equating 'REST' with 'uses HTTP and JSON' — missing statelessness and HATEOAS
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Richardson Maturity Model (Level 0-3) and that most APIs are Level 2 (resources + HTTP verbs), not Level 3 (HATEOAS)

sections.title: Most APIs Claim to Be RESTful — Almost None Actually Are
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is equating REST with "uses HTTP and returns JSON.
- REST is an **architectural style defined by six constraints**, and most production APIs satisfy only two or three of them.
- Roy Fielding's dissertation defines REST as a set of constraints that, when all applied together, produce the scalability and evolvability properties of the web.

The **Richardson Maturity Model** measures how RESTful an API actually is.
- Level 0 is a single endpoint with POST for everything (RPC over HTTP).
- Level 1 introduces individual resources with unique URIs.
- Level 2 adds proper HTTP verbs and status codes — **this is where most production APIs stop.** Level 3 adds HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State), where responses include links to related resources and available actions.
- Very few APIs reach Level 3 because the client needs to understand hypermedia navigation, which most frontend teams find unnecessary overhead.

Understanding the constraints matters in interviews because it shows you know the difference between "an API that uses HTTP" and "a RESTful API" — and can articulate why most teams deliberately choose Level 2 as the pragmatic sweet spot.

sections.title: The Six REST Constraints — What Each Requires and What Breaks Without It
sections.content:
Each constraint exists to solve a specific distributed systems problem. Knowing the constraint is the easy part — knowing what breaks without it is what interviewers test.

| Constraint | What It Requires | What Breaks Without It |
|---|---|---|
| **Client-Server** | Separate client and server concerns | Tight coupling prevents independent deployment |
| **Stateless** | Each request carries all info needed; no server-side session | Horizontal scaling requires sticky sessions or shared state |
| **Cacheable** | Responses declare cacheability via headers | Every request hits the server; CDNs can't help |
| **Uniform Interface** | Resources identified by URIs, manipulated through representations | Clients need custom logic per endpoint |
| **Layered System** | Client can't tell if it's connected to the origin or intermediary | Proxies, gateways, and load balancers can't be inserted transparently |
| **Code on Demand** (optional) | Server can send executable code (JavaScript) | Not typically used in APIs; the only optional constraint |

**Statelessness is the constraint most APIs violate** without realizing it. If your API requires a server-side session for authentication (storing session ID in memory), you've broken statelessness. JWT tokens solve this by carrying authentication state in the token itself — the server doesn't need to remember anything between requests.

sections.title: Why Level 2 Is the Pragmatic Choice and When HATEOAS Actually Helps
sections.content:
Most teams stop at Level 2 (resources + HTTP verbs + status codes) because the cost of implementing HATEOAS outweighs its benefits for most applications. HATEOAS means every response includes links to related resources and available state transitions — an order response would include links to cancel, pay, or view the associated customer.

**HATEOAS genuinely helps in two scenarios:** APIs consumed by third-party developers who shouldn't hardcode URLs (because you'll change them), and APIs where the available actions depend on resource state (an order can only be cancelled before shipping). For internal APIs with tightly coupled clients, HATEOAS adds serialization overhead and complexity without meaningful benefit.

In interview context, the right answer isn't "HATEOAS is required for REST" or "nobody uses HATEOAS." It's: **"Level 2 REST with proper resources, verbs, and status codes is the industry standard. HATEOAS is valuable when API discoverability matters, but most teams deliberately choose pragmatism over purity."**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **REST is 6 constraints, not just HTTP + JSON** — statelessness, client-server, uniform interface, layered system, cacheable, and optionally code-on-demand; most APIs calling themselves 'REST' only implement the uniform interface.
- **Statelessness is the hardest constraint to enforce in practice** — every request must carry all state needed to process it; server-side sessions violate statelessness and prevent horizontal scaling.
- **Richardson Maturity Model Level 2 ≠ fully RESTful** — Level 2 (HTTP verbs + resource URIs) is what most APIs implement; Level 3 (HATEOAS) is the actual REST constraint; very few production APIs reach Level 3.
- **Uniform interface = resource-based URIs, not action-based** — `/orders/123/cancel` (action) violates the constraint; `/orders/123` + `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}` is correct.
- **Cacheability requires `Cache-Control` headers** — `GET` responses without `Cache-Control` are technically non-compliant; explicitly setting `Cache-Control: no-cache` or `max-age` makes cacheable responses explicit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
REST is not a protocol or a library — it is an architectural style defined by six constraints. The term is widely misused: most APIs described as 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs that partially follow REST principles.

**The constraints that matter in interviews**
- **Stateless** — every request contains all information needed to process it; the server holds no session state; this constraint is what enables horizontal scaling without sticky sessions
- **Uniform interface** — resources identified by URI, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, and HATEOAS; the uniform interface is what defines REST, not just using HTTP
- **Layered system** — client cannot tell if it is talking directly to the server or through a proxy, load balancer, or CDN; enables transparent infrastructure changes

**Richardson Maturity Model**
- Level 0: single URI, all operations via POST (SOAP-style)
- Level 1: separate resources (`/orders`, `/customers`)
- Level 2: HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) + correct status codes — this is what most 'REST APIs' actually implement
- Level 3: HATEOAS — responses contain links to related actions; clients discover capabilities rather than hardcoding URIs

Resource-based URIs represent things, not actions: `/orders/123/cancel` is action-based; `/orders/123` with `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}` is resource-based and the correct pattern.

questions.question: How do you decide which HTTP status code to return? Walk me through the most important ones.
questions.title: HTTP Status Codes — Decision Guide for REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: Use **2xx** for success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 4xx for client errors (400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 unauthorized, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable), 5xx for server errors (500 internal, 503 unavailable).

interviewer_intent.testing: Correct usage of 401 vs 403, 400 vs 422, 200 vs 204
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 200 for everything including errors, or returning 400 for all validation errors instead of 422
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the semantic distinction between 401 (not authenticated) and 403 (authenticated but not authorized)

sections.title: Status Codes Are Semantic Contracts — Not Just Numbers for Success and Failure
sections.content:
The most common API mistake is returning 200 for everything — including errors wrapped in a JSON body like `{"success": false, "error": "Not found"}`.
- This breaks HTTP semantics because proxies, caches, and monitoring tools rely on status codes to make decisions.
- **A CDN caches 200 responses.** If your 200 response contains an error, clients cache the error.

The second most common mistake is confusing **401 (Unauthenticated) with 403 (Unauthorized).** 401 means "I don't know who you are — send credentials." 403 means "I know who you are, and you don't have permission.
- The response to 401 should include a `WWW-Authenticate` header telling the client how to authenticate.
- The response to 403 should never include that header — the client is already authenticated.

Another subtle distinction is **400 (Bad Request) vs 422 (Unprocessable Entity).** 400 means the request is syntactically malformed — bad JSON, missing required headers. 422 means the syntax is valid but the content is semantically wrong — trying to create a user with an email that already exists. Most APIs use 400 for both, which is acceptable but less precise.

sections.title: The Status Codes That Matter in Interviews — Grouped by Decision
sections.content:
Instead of memorizing all codes, learn the **decision points** — when you're building an endpoint, these are the choices you actually make.

| Decision | Code | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Success — created something** | 201 Created | POST that created a resource; include `Location` header |
| **Success — no body** | 204 No Content | DELETE or PUT that succeeded with nothing to return |
| **Success — standard** | 200 OK | GET, PUT/PATCH with response body |
| **Client sent bad syntax** | 400 Bad Request | Malformed JSON, missing required fields |
| **Not authenticated** | 401 Unauthorized | No credentials or expired token; include `WWW-Authenticate` |
| **Authenticated but forbidden** | 403 Forbidden | Valid user, insufficient permissions |
| **Resource doesn't exist** | 404 Not Found | ID not found, or hiding 403 for security |
| **Method not allowed** | 405 Method Not Allowed | POST to a read-only resource |
| **Conflict with current state** | 409 Conflict | Duplicate creation, optimistic locking failure |
| **Validation error** | 422 Unprocessable Entity | Valid syntax but semantically wrong data |
| **Rate limited** | 429 Too Many Requests | Include `Retry-After` header |
| **Server error** | 500 Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception — never expose stack traces |

**The `Location` header on 201 is frequently overlooked** — after creating a resource, the response should include `Location: /api/users/42` pointing to the newly created resource.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **401 vs 403: authentication vs authorization** — `401 Unauthorized` means no valid credentials presented (should authenticate); `403 Forbidden` means credentials are valid but the user lacks permission.
- **`422 Unprocessable Entity` for business rule violations; `400 Bad Request` for malformed input** — a syntactically valid JSON body with an invalid business value is `422`, not `400`.
- **`201 Created` must include a `Location` header** — `Location: /orders/456` tells the client where the new resource lives; returning `200` for a create operation is semantically wrong.
- **`409 Conflict` for optimistic locking failures and duplicate resource creation** — not `400`; the request was well-formed but conflicts with current state.
- **`204 No Content` for successful DELETE and PUT with no response body** — returning `200` with an empty body is ambiguous; `204` explicitly signals 'success, nothing to return'.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP status codes are a contract with API clients. Returning `200` for everything or `400` for all errors forces clients to parse the response body to understand what happened — defeating the purpose of the protocol.

**The decision tree**
- `200 OK` — successful GET, successful PATCH/PUT with response body
- `201 Created` — successful POST that created a resource; must include `Location: /resource/id` header
- `204 No Content` — successful DELETE or PUT with no body to return
- `400 Bad Request` — malformed request syntax, invalid JSON, missing required field that prevents parsing
- `401 Unauthorized` — no credentials provided or credentials invalid; client should authenticate
- `403 Forbidden` — credentials valid, but insufficient permission for this resource or operation
- `404 Not Found` — resource does not exist; also used intentionally to hide existence of restricted resources
- `409 Conflict` — optimistic lock conflict, duplicate key, state machine violation
- `422 Unprocessable Entity` — syntactically valid request, but violates business rules (transfer amount exceeds balance)
- `429 Too Many Requests` — rate limit exceeded; include `Retry-After` header

The `401` vs `403` distinction is the most common interview checkpoint: `401` = 'I don't know who you are'; `403` = 'I know who you are, but no'.

questions.question: What is idempotency in REST APIs? Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.title: Idempotency in REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: An operation is **idempotent** if calling it multiple times produces the same result as calling it once. **GET**, **PUT**, **DELETE**, and HEAD are idempotent. **POST** is not. **PATCH** may or may not be, depending on implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand idempotency for retry safety and distributed systems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying DELETE is not idempotent because the second call returns 404 — the resource state is the same (deleted), so it is idempotent
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency keys for POST operations (Stripe's approach for payment APIs)

sections.title: Idempotency Isn't About the Response Code — It's About the Resource State
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is saying DELETE is not idempotent because the second call returns 404. **Idempotency is about the final state of the resource, not the response code.** After the first DELETE, the resource is gone. After the second DELETE, the resource is still gone. The server state is identical — that's idempotent.

GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent by specification. **POST is not** — calling POST twice creates two resources. This is why payment APIs use idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with each POST, and the server returns the same response for duplicate keys instead of processing the request again.

**PATCH is the nuanced case.** A patch that says "set status to ACTIVE" is idempotent — applying it twice produces the same state.
- A patch that says "increment counter by 1" is not — applying it twice produces a different state.
- Whether PATCH is idempotent depends entirely on the operation, not the method.

sections.title: HTTP Method Contracts — Safety, Idempotency, and What Infrastructure Assumes
sections.content:
These properties aren't just theoretical — they determine how proxies, load balancers, and API gateways treat your requests. Getting them wrong means infrastructure that was supposed to help you (retry logic, caching) actively works against you.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Typical Use | Infrastructure Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | ✅ | ✅ | Read resource | Cached by CDN; safe to retry indefinitely |
| HEAD | ✅ | ✅ | Check existence/headers | Same as GET without body |
| PUT | ❌ | ✅ | Replace entire resource | Load balancer may retry on failure |
| DELETE | ❌ | ✅ | Remove resource | Safe to retry — second call returns 404, state is same |
| POST | ❌ | ❌ | Create resource, trigger action | Never cached; never retried automatically |
| PATCH | ❌ | Depends | Partial update | Not retried automatically — idempotency depends on operation |

**The retry column is the practical consequence.** A load balancer that loses the connection after sending a PUT request can safely retry it — sending the same replacement payload twice produces the same final state. A load balancer that loses the connection after sending a POST cannot retry it safely — the operation may have already executed, and retrying would create a duplicate. This is exactly why payment processing APIs use idempotency keys with POST rather than switching to PUT — the semantics of POST (create a new resource) are correct for payments, but the retry problem requires a separate solution.

sections.title: Idempotency Keys — How Stripe Solves the Duplicate Payment Problem
sections.content:
POST endpoints create resources, and network failures make retries dangerous. If a client sends a payment request and the connection drops before receiving the response, the payment may have been processed but the client doesn't know. Retrying could charge the customer twice.

**Idempotency keys** solve this. The client generates a unique key (typically a UUID) and sends it in a header like `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The server stores the key with the response. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the stored response without re-executing the logic.

The implementation requires careful decisions: **how long to store keys** (Stripe stores them for 24 hours), **what storage to use** (Redis for distributed systems, database for durability), and **what to do when a key matches but the request body differs** (Stripe returns 422 — the key can't be reused for a different operation).
- This pattern is essential for any API where duplicate execution has financial or data integrity consequences.

sections.title: Idempotency-Key Pattern — Stripe-Style Server Dedup
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Idempotent ≠ safe** — safe = no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS); idempotent = same result on repeat (GET, PUT, DELETE, PATCH when absolute); POST is neither safe nor idempotent.
- **DELETE returning `404` on the second call is still idempotent** — idempotency is about server state, not response code; the resource is absent in both cases — that is the consistent outcome.
- **POST with an idempotency key makes it idempotent** — Stripe, PayPal, and AWS use `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` headers; the server stores the first result and returns it for duplicate requests.
- **PATCH is idempotent only if it uses absolute assignment** — `PATCH {"status": "active"}` is idempotent; `PATCH {"count": "+1"}` is not.
- **Retrying non-idempotent operations causes duplicate processing** — network timeouts on POST requests without idempotency keys charge customers twice, create duplicate orders, or send duplicate emails.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Idempotency means calling an operation multiple times has the same effect on server state as calling it once. It is the property that makes safe retries possible — critical for distributed systems where network failures and timeouts are normal.

**Which methods are idempotent by spec**
- GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — safe and idempotent (read-only, no side effects)
- PUT — idempotent: `PUT /orders/123 {"status": "shipped"}` sets the same state every time
- DELETE — idempotent: the resource is absent after the first call; subsequent calls may return `404` but the state (resource absent) is consistent
- POST — not idempotent by default; each call may create a new resource

**Making POST idempotent**
- The client generates a UUID and sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` with the request
- The server stores the result keyed by the idempotency key (typically in Redis with a TTL)
- Duplicate requests within the TTL window return the stored result without reprocessing
- Stripe uses this for payment operations — the client can retry safely on timeout without charging the customer twice

A PATCH operation's idempotency depends on the semantics: `{"status": "active"}` is idempotent (absolute assignment); `{"balance": "+10"}` is not (relative change).

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH in REST APIs?
questions.title: PUT vs PATCH — When to Use Each in REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: **PUT** replaces the entire resource with the payload you send. **PATCH** applies a partial update to specific fields. PUT is **idempotent** by definition; PATCH is technically not guaranteed to be idempotent, though most implementations make it so in practice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the semantic difference and can explain the idempotency nuance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PUT for partial updates — sending only changed fields with PUT technically violates REST semantics because PUT should replace the entire resource.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that PATCH can be idempotent if implemented as absolute field assignments, but is not idempotent for relative operations like incrementing a counter.

sections.title: PUT Replaces the Entire Resource — PATCH Only Changes What You Send
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is **replacement vs modification.** PUT sends a complete representation of the resource — every field must be included. If you omit a field, it should be set to null or its default. PATCH sends only the fields that should change, leaving everything else untouched.

The most common mistake is using PUT for partial updates — sending only changed fields with PUT **technically violates REST semantics** because PUT is defined as a complete replacement. In practice, many APIs accept partial PUT requests, but an interviewer asking this question wants you to know the specification-level distinction.

The practical consequence: **PUT is idempotent by definition** — sending the same complete representation twice produces the same state.
- PATCH can be idempotent if implemented as absolute field assignments ("set name to Alice"), but is not idempotent if implemented as relative operations ("append 'Jr.' to name").
- This makes PUT safer for retries without idempotency keys.

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH — When Each Is the Right Choice
sections.content:
The choice affects idempotency, payload size, and how the server processes the request.

| Aspect | PUT | PATCH |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantics** | Replace the entire resource | Modify specific fields |
| **Payload** | Complete representation (all fields) | Only changed fields |
| **Missing fields** | Set to null/default | Left unchanged |
| **Idempotent** | Always | Depends on operation type |
| **Retry safety** | Safe without idempotency key | May need idempotency key |
| **Bandwidth** | Higher (full resource) | Lower (only changes) |
| **When to use** | Simple resources, replace workflows | Large resources, partial updates |

**In practice, PATCH dominates** for API updates because most updates change one or two fields of a large resource. Requiring the client to send the entire user object just to update an email address wastes bandwidth and creates race conditions — two clients reading the same user, changing different fields, and PUTting back will overwrite each other's changes. PATCH avoids this because each client sends only the field it changed.

sections.title: Why PATCH Is the Safer Default — And the Race Condition PUT Creates With Concurrent Writers
sections.content:
**Use PATCH as your default for update endpoints.** Most updates change one or two fields of a resource that has ten or twenty. Requiring clients to send the complete resource representation for every update creates bandwidth waste, client complexity, and a subtle but serious race condition.

The race condition: Client A reads a user, Client B reads the same user, Client A changes the email and PUTs the full resource, Client B changes the role and PUTs the full resource. Client B's PUT was based on the original state — it includes the old email in its payload. **Client B's update silently overwrites Client A's change.** With PATCH, Client B only sends `{"role": "admin"}` — Client A's email change is preserved.

**Use PUT when the client is replacing an entire resource and you want the idempotency guarantee without an idempotency key.** Configuration objects are a natural fit — replacing a user's notification preferences completely is conceptually a PUT: the client sends the entire new preference set and the old state is discarded. The idempotency guarantee means load balancers can retry without consequence.

For PATCH, the RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch format is the simplest approach — send a JSON object with only the fields to change, and null to explicitly clear a field. RFC 6902 JSON Patch is more expressive (supports array operations, copy, move) but significantly more complex for clients to construct. Most APIs implement Merge Patch and only reach for JSON Patch when they need fine-grained array manipulation.

sections.title: PUT Full Replacement vs PATCH JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch
Key Points
sections.content:
- **PUT = full replacement; PATCH = partial update** — PUT with a partial body technically replaces the resource with the partial representation, nulling out missing fields; PATCH applies only the specified changes.
- **PUT is idempotent; PATCH is idempotent only with absolute assignment** — `PATCH {"status": "active"}` is idempotent; `PATCH {"views": "+1"}` is not.
- **Spring MVC: `@PutMapping` vs `@PatchMapping`** — routing-level distinction; actual idempotency behavior is your implementation's responsibility.
- **JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is the formal PATCH specification** — operations: `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy`, `test`; most APIs implement a simpler 'merge patch' instead.
- **The practical danger of misusing PUT** — a client that does not know about all fields sends `PUT /users/1 {"name": "Alice"}` and wipes `email`, `phone`, and `address` silently; use PATCH for partial updates.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PUT and PATCH both modify resources, but they have fundamentally different semantics that affect how clients must construct requests and how servers must process them.

**PUT — full replacement**
- The request body is the complete new representation of the resource
- Fields missing from the body are treated as null or removed from the resource
- `PUT /users/1 {"name": "Alice"}` — if the server follows PUT semantics strictly, `email` and `phone` are wiped
- Clients must fetch the current state first, modify the fields they want, then PUT the complete object — expensive and racey

**PATCH — partial update**
- Only the fields present in the request body are modified; absent fields are untouched
- More bandwidth-efficient: only send what changed
- Idempotent when using absolute assignment (`"status": "active"`); not idempotent with relative changes (`"count": "+1"`)

**JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch**
- Merge Patch (RFC 7396): simple JSON object, fields present replace existing values, null values delete fields — this is what most APIs implement
- JSON Patch (RFC 6902): array of operation objects (`add`, `remove`, `replace`) — powerful but verbose; used when atomic multi-field operations matter

In practice: use PUT when clients always know the complete state (rare), PATCH for any partial update (most common).

questions.question: What are the HTTP methods GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH, and when should each be used in a REST API?
questions.title: HTTP Methods Deep Dive — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH Semantics
questions.direct_answer: Each **HTTP method** maps to a CRUD operation with specific semantics: **GET** retrieves (safe, **idempotent**, cacheable), **POST** creates (not idempotent), **PUT** replaces entirely (idempotent), **PATCH** modifies partially (**idempotency** depends on operation), **DELETE** removes (idempotent). Using methods correctly enables caching, safe retries, and clear API semantics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the semantic meaning of each method beyond simple CRUD mapping.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using POST for everything — losing idempotency guarantees, caching, and clear API semantics.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain safety (GET doesn't modify state) vs idempotency (PUT can be retried safely), and mention that POST tunneling (using POST for everything) is a REST anti-pattern.

sections.title: HTTP Methods Are Not CRUD Labels — They're Contracts With Infrastructure
sections.content:
Most developers learn HTTP methods as CRUD shortcuts: GET = read, POST = create, PUT = update, DELETE = delete.
- This mental model works for simple APIs but misses the properties that actually matter: **safety** and **idempotency**.
- These properties aren't just theoretical — they determine how proxies cache responses, whether load balancers can retry failed requests, and how API gateways handle traffic.

A **safe** method doesn't modify server state. GET and HEAD are safe — calling them has no side effects. This is why browsers pre-fetch links, search engines crawl your URLs, and CDNs cache GET responses. If your GET endpoint modifies data (a common anti-pattern), caches serve stale data and crawlers trigger unintended writes.

An **idempotent** method produces the same result regardless of how many times it's called.
- GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent.
- POST is not.
- This is why load balancers can safely retry a failed PUT — sending it twice doesn't create two resources.
- Retrying a failed POST, however, might create a duplicate.
- Understanding this distinction is the difference between designing APIs that work reliably with infrastructure and ones that fight it.

sections.title: Method Properties — What Infrastructure Assumes About Each Method
sections.content:
| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Body | Typical Use | Infrastructure Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | ✅ | ✅ | No | Retrieve resource | Cached by CDNs and proxies |
| POST | ❌ | ❌ | Yes | Create resource, trigger action | Never cached, never retried automatically |
| PUT | ❌ | ✅ | Yes | Replace entire resource | Safe to retry on failure |
| PATCH | ❌ | Depends | Yes | Partial update | Not guaranteed idempotent |
| DELETE | ❌ | ✅ | Optional | Remove resource | Safe to retry on failure |
| HEAD | ✅ | ✅ | No | Check resource existence | Same as GET without body |

The "Infrastructure Behavior" column is why method choice matters beyond semantics. Using POST for an idempotent operation means your load balancer won't retry it on failure — you lose automatic resilience that PUT and DELETE get for free.

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH vs POST — The Decision That Reveals Your Understanding
sections.content:
The most common follow-up: "when do you use PUT vs PATCH?" The answer reveals whether you've thought about partial updates.

**PUT replaces the entire resource.** If you PUT a user with only `name` and `email`, every other field becomes null (or its default). This is the contract — the request body IS the new state. PUT is idempotent because sending the same request twice produces the same result.

**PATCH modifies specific fields.** Only the fields in the request body change; everything else stays.
- PATCH is NOT inherently idempotent — a PATCH that says "increment counter by 1" gives a different result each time.
- A PATCH that says "set name to John" is idempotent.
- The idempotency depends on the operation, not the method.

**POST is the catch-all.** It creates resources, triggers actions, processes payments — anything that doesn't fit the other methods.
- The key constraint: POST is not idempotent and not safe.
- Using POST for everything ("POST tunneling") throws away the guarantees that GET, PUT, and DELETE give you.
- Caches don't work, retries aren't safe, and API documentation loses clarity.

In Spring MVC, the mapping is explicit: `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`. Using the correct annotation isn't just convention — it generates accurate OpenAPI documentation and enables Spring Security's method-level security to work correctly.

sections.title: curl Example per HTTP Method
sections.content:
# --- GET: read a resource (safe, idempotent, cacheable) -----------------------
curl -s https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42
# -> 200 OK with the order JSON

# Conditional GET (cache revalidation)
curl -s https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42 \
     -H 'If-None-Match: "v3"'
# -> 304 Not Modified  (no body)

# --- POST: create a resource (not idempotent unless you add Idempotency-Key) --
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H 'Idempotency-Key: 7a9c3f12-b4e8-4e0a-9f77-0b3a8c2d1e55' \
     -d '{ "sku": "ABC-123", "qty": 2 }'
# -> 201 Created
# Location: /v1/orders/ord_abcd

# --- PUT: full replacement (idempotent) ---------------------------------------
curl -X PUT https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42 \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H 'If-Match: "v3"' \
     -d '{ "id": 42, "sku": "ABC-123", "qty": 3, "status": "paid" }'
# -> 200 OK (or 204 No Content). Same body twice = same state.

# --- PATCH: partial update (idempotency not guaranteed) -----------------------
curl -X PATCH https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42 \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json' \
     -d '{ "status": "shipped" }'
# -> 200 OK

# --- DELETE: remove the resource (idempotent) --------------------------------
curl -X DELETE https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42
# -> 204 No Content on first call
# -> 204 No Content (or 404) on subsequent calls — server choice; still idempotent

# --- HEAD: metadata only, no body (used for cache checks, existence checks) ---
curl -I https://api.example.com/v1/orders/42
# -> 200 OK
# Content-Length: 1823
# ETag: "v3"

# --- OPTIONS: capabilities / CORS preflight ----------------------------------
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
     -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
     -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST'
# -> 204 No Content
# Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
# Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization, Idempotency-Key

# Quick properties table:
#   Method  Safe  Idempotent  Cacheable  Typical status
#   GET     yes   yes         yes        200 / 304
#   HEAD    yes   yes         yes        200
#   POST    no    no*         rare       201 (with Location)
#   PUT     no    yes         no         200 / 204
#   PATCH   no    no**        no         200 / 204
#   DELETE  no    yes         no         204 / 200 / 202
# *  POST becomes idempotent-like when paired with Idempotency-Key and server dedup.
# ** PATCH is idempotent for whole-field set ops; not for append/array-push ops.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GET and HEAD are safe and idempotent; DELETE and PUT are idempotent but not safe** — safe = no side effects; idempotent = same state result on repeat; POST is neither.
- **GET must not have a request body** — some frameworks allow it, but HTTP/1.1 semantics say GET body has no defined meaning; use query parameters or POST for complex query criteria.
- **PUT sends the full resource representation; PATCH sends a partial update** — a PUT with a partial body nulls out missing fields; PATCH applies only what is present.
- **DELETE returning `404` on the second call is still idempotent** — server state (resource absent) is the same; only the response code differs.
- **OPTIONS is the preflight method for CORS** — browsers send `OPTIONS` before cross-origin non-simple requests; the server must respond with allowed methods and origins or the actual request is blocked.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP methods are not just routing conventions — they carry semantic contracts about idempotency, safety, and caching that clients, proxies, and CDNs rely on.

**The four dimensions**
- **Safe** — no server-side state change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
- **Idempotent** — same server state on repeated calls: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE
- **Cacheable** — responses may be cached: GET, HEAD (by default), POST with explicit headers
- **Request body allowed** — semantic convention: POST, PUT, PATCH (yes); GET, DELETE (technically allowed but semantically undefined)

**Decision guide**
- Retrieve a resource or collection → GET
- Create a new resource (server assigns ID) → POST
- Replace a resource completely (client knows ID) → PUT
- Partially modify a resource → PATCH
- Remove a resource → DELETE
- Discover available methods (CORS preflight) → OPTIONS

**Common mistakes**
- POST for everything: loses idempotency and cacheability signals for clients and CDNs
- GET with a request body for complex search: use POST to `/orders/search` with a request body for complex filter criteria — GET body is semantically undefined
- DELETE that is not idempotent: throwing `404` on the second call is fine; the state (resource gone) is the same
